plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Downs cell, the industrial electrolytic apparatus used to produce pure sodium metal from molten sodium chloride via the reaction 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The cell interior contains a bath of molten NaCl, with a cylindrical iron screen separating the electrode compartments; the cathode (−) occupies the outer annular region and the anode (+) projects upward from the bottom center, both connected to an external voltage source at the lower right. Liquid sodium metal, which is less dense than the molten salt, rises and collects in a side reservoir on the right, from which it drains through a labeled Na outlet; simultaneously, Cl2 gas produced at the anode rises through a central green-tinted collector tube and exits through a labeled Cl2 outlet at the upper right, while fresh NaCl is fed continuously through an inlet at the top. The iron screen physically segregates the two products — liquid sodium and gaseous chlorine — preventing their recombination and enabling continuous, separate collection of each. This figure demonstrates the Downs cell as the industrial-scale process for sodium production and explains why aqueous electrolysis cannot substitute for it, since H+ ions are more easily reduced than Na+ ions at any cathode in contact with water.

demo_steps.title: Identify the cell layout
demo_steps.narration: The cell contains molten NaCl, not an aqueous solution, so Na+ and Cl− are the ions being electrolyzed. The central anode is separated from the outer cathode region by an iron screen.

demo_steps.title: Run the electrolysis
demo_steps.narration: As current flows, Cl− migrates inward to the anode and forms Cl2 gas, while Na+ migrates outward to the cathode and forms liquid sodium. The animation shows chlorine rising through the central outlet and sodium collecting in the side outlet.

demo_steps.title: Click the electrodes
demo_steps.narration: Click the anode to see the oxidation half-reaction, then click the cathode to see the reduction half-reaction. Together they add to the overall Downs cell reaction.

demo_steps.title: See why separation matters
demo_steps.narration: The iron screen keeps newly formed sodium metal away from chlorine gas. Without this physical separation, the products could recombine to form NaCl again.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The Downs cell works because molten NaCl supplies Na+ and Cl− directly, and the apparatus continuously separates the sodium and chlorine products as they form.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate a labeled 2D cross-section similar to the textbook figure: gray cell walls, pale lavender molten NaCl bath, central brown anode, outer cathode contacts, black mesh iron screen, green chlorine collector rising upward to a Cl2 outlet, and a right-side pink sodium collection chamber draining to a Na outlet. Use arrows and small moving ion symbols to show Cl− moving toward the central anode and Na+ moving toward the outer cathode. When an electrode is clicked, highlight that region with a bright outline and place its balanced half-reaction in a nearby callout. Keep the iron screen visually prominent because it explains product separation.

authoredContext:
The most important method for the production of sodium is the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride; the set-up is a Downs cell , shown in . The reaction involved in this process is:

Separation of the molten sodium and chlorine prevents recombination. The liquid sodium, which is less dense than molten sodium chloride, floats to the surface and flows into a collector. The gaseous chlorine goes to storage tanks. Chlorine is also a valuable product.

Pure sodium metal is isolated by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using a Downs cell. It is not possible to isolate sodium by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of sodium salts because hydrogen ions are more easily reduced than are sodium ions; as a result, hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of the desired sodium metal. The high temperature required to melt NaCl means that liquid sodium metal forms.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram is a T-shaped structure labeled, “Anode ( positive sign ),” that is on a mesh-like background labeled, “Iron screen.” The anode is connected to a box labeled, “Voltage source,” by a line, and the voltage source is connected to one of two L-shaped structures that surround the anode. They are labeled, “Cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the cathode on the right side of the diagram is a tube connected to a collection chamber labeled, “N a metal,” that has a lower outlet labeled, “N a outlet.” Surrounding all of these components is a blue background labeled, “Molten N a C l,” and a series of tubes that form a square outside the diagram. They have an opening in the upper right corner labeled, “Inlet for N a C l.” At the top of the diagram is a large tube with an upward-facing arrow drawn on it. The tube turns right, has a right-facing arrow on it, and is labeled, “C l subscript 2 outlet.”

discrepancies: The default view adds many large labeled Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ion disks over the cell; the source shows only small pale green bubbles/particles and no large ion labels, so the mesh and electrodes are partially obscured.
The outer steel cell is simplified into a mostly rectangular tank, missing several stepped wall/base details and side flanges visible in the source.

The central green chlorine collector/riser is not shaped like the source: the generated version has a broad diagonal collector manifold and altered proportions rather than the cleaner vertical riser with top elbow.
The sodium collection chamber and outlet are only approximate; its contours and necking differ noticeably from the source and the outlet/label spacing is less faithful.
The NaCl inlet assembly is simplified and somewhat misproportioned compared with the small raised inlet structure in the source.
Extra pedagogical overlays and hidden/interactive reaction callouts are not part of the original static figure and change the default visual style when ion markers are visible.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is clearly recognizable as the same Downs cell and includes useful interactions, but the default image is cluttered by added ion disks and several vessel/pipe geometries are only approximate.
action_items: Hide the large Na⁺/Cl⁻ ion disks in the default static state, or make them much smaller and reveal them only when the electrolysis animation is enabled.
Redraw the outer tank with the source’s stepped base, side walls, flanges, and grey wall proportions rather than a simplified rectangle.
Refine the central chlorine pipe/collector to match the source’s vertical riser, tapered internal arrow, and top right outlet geometry.
Adjust the sodium chamber, NaCl inlet, and outlet positions/proportions to more closely match the original layout.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are strong, but the critic identifies generator-level hallucinated overlays and geometry/proportion refinements that can be fixed without changing the plan.
